desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

All values in the list are distinct. In one move you may detach any single node and re-attach it either at the very front (as the new head) or at the very back (as the new tail). Return the minimum number of moves needed to make the list sorted in increasing order.

Example: [2,3,4,1] needs 1 move (send 1 to the front). [3,1,2,4] needs 2 moves (send 3 to the back, then 4 to the back).
hints: Moving each node at most once is always enough. So ask the opposite question: which nodes can you afford to leave untouched?

The untouched nodes keep their relative order, and every moved node ends up at one of the two ends. So the untouched nodes must already appear in increasing order, and nothing that is moved may belong between two untouched values.

That means the untouched values are consecutive values of the sorted order (ranks r, r+1, ..., r+L-1) and in the list they appear left to right in that order. Maximise L; the answer is n - L. Compute each value's position and its rank, then scan the ranks once keeping a running chain length.
editorial: Let rank(x) be the position of x in sorted order and pos(x) its index in the list. Suppose some set U of nodes is never moved. Every other node is moved once to the front or to the back, so in the final list the nodes smaller than all of U can be placed in front and the larger ones behind, but a moved node whose value lies between two untouched values would have to sit between them, which is impossible because it is only ever placed at an end. Hence U must be a block of consecutive ranks, and for the final list to be sorted its members must already be in increasing order of position.

Conversely any such block can be kept: send the smaller values to the front and the larger values to the back in the right order (smaller ones from the largest to the smallest to the front, larger ones from the smallest to the largest to the back). So the answer is n - L where L is the longest run of consecutive ranks with pos(rank r) < pos(rank r+1) < ....
Sort once to get the ranks (O(n log n)), then a single scan computes the longest such run in O(n). The extra space is O(n) for the position table.
